If an illness or accident leaves you unable to speak or make decisions, someone still has to decide what medical care you receive and how your financial affairs are handled. An advance directive and power of attorney can prepare for those situations, but they serve different purposes. Knowing how each works and the role they play can help you avoid gaps in your estate plan and give your family clearer instructions when difficult decisions arise.


[A financial advisor can help you review](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=advancedirectivevspowerofattorney) **how powers of attorney, beneficiary designations and other estate-planning decisions fit into your broader financial plan.**


## What an Advance Directive Covers


An[advance directive](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/what-is-an-advance-directive) is a legal document that states your preferences for medical care if you become unable to communicate or make healthcare decisions yourself. Depending on the state and the form being used, an advance directive may also be referred to as a living will, or it may include a living will as one part of a broader healthcare planning document.


The document can address decisions such as whether you want cardiopulmonary resuscitation, mechanical ventilation, artificial nutrition and hydration, pain management or other life-sustaining treatment. It can also provide guidance about end-of-life care if you are terminally ill, permanently unconscious or facing another condition in which recovery is unlikely.


One important feature of an advance directive is that it can state your wishes directly. Rather than relying entirely on another person to decide what you would have wanted, the document gives physicians, hospital staff and family members written instructions to follow when the circumstances described in the directive apply.


That can reduce uncertainty at a stressful time. For example, if your directive clearly says that you do not want life-sustaining treatment under specific medical conditions, healthcare providers can use that instruction under those conditions, subject to applicable state law and medical requirements.


## An Example of an Advance Directive in Practice


Suppose a patient suffers a catastrophic medical event and is diagnosed as being in an irreversible coma with no meaningful brain activity. The patient’s advance directive states that they would like life-sustaining treatment withheld if there is no reasonable expectation of recovery.


Medical Situation Instruction in the Advance Directive Who Follows It


Patient is in an irreversible coma with no meaningful brain activity and no reasonable expectation of recovery Withhold or discontinue life-sustaining treatment, including mechanical ventilation, consistent with the directive Attending physicians, hospital staff and other healthcare providers


In this example, the directive provides the patient’s instruction in advance. The healthcare team does not necessarily need a separate person to invent or interpret the patient’s preference because the document already addresses the situation directly.


However, real medical situations do not always fit neatly into language written years earlier. That is one reason people often opt to pair an advance directive with a healthcare power of attorney.


## What a Power of Attorney Covers


A[power of attorney (POA)](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/does-next-of-kin-override-power-of-attorney) is a legal document that gives another person authority to act on your behalf. The person granting the authority is generally called the principal, while the person appointed to act is commonly called the agent or attorney-in-fact.


It’s possible to write a POA either broadly or narrowly. For instance, a financial power of attorney might authorize an agent to pay bills, manage investments, handle banking transactions, file taxes, deal with insurance companies or manage real estate. A healthcare power of attorney, meanwhile, could authorize an agent to make medical decisions when you cannot make those decisions yourself.


One of the most important distinctions is whether the power of attorney is durable. A[durable power of attorney](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/durable-vs-general-power-of-attorney) remains effective, or becomes effective, depending on its terms, when the principal becomes incapacitated. That makes durability particularly important for[estate and incapacity planning](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/estate-planning-essentials) .


A non-durable power of attorney, in contrast, typically terminates if the principal becomes incapacitated. Non-durable POAs may be useful for temporary or limited transactions. This could include a situation such as allowing someone to complete a real estate closing while you are unavailable. However, they generally do not provide the same protection for long-term incapacity planning.


Because the goal of an estate plan is often to prepare for the possibility that you may someday be unable to manage your own affairs, durable powers of attorney are common tools in both financial and healthcare planning.


## How a Healthcare Power of Attorney Differs From an Advance Directive


An advance directive and healthcare power of attorney both deal with medical decisions, but they work differently. An advance directive records your own instructions about treatments and medical situations in advance. Meanwhile, a healthcare power of attorney appoints someone who can make decisions for you.


That distinction becomes important when your advance directive does not specifically cover a medical situation. A healthcare agent can consider your stated wishes, conversations you had before becoming incapacitated and the details of your current condition when deciding how to proceed.


For example, an advance directive might say whether you want artificial life support if recovery is impossible, but it may not address every surgery, treatment option, medication or rehabilitation decision that could arise. A healthcare agent can make those judgment calls when the document itself does not provide a clear answer.


Feature Advance Directive Healthcare Power of Attorney Financial Power of Attorney


What It Covers Medical treatment preferences, including end-of-life care Medical and healthcare decisions Financial, legal and property matters


Who Makes Decisions Your written instructions generally guide providers directly An appointed healthcare agent An appointed financial agent


When It Takes Effect Generally when applicable medical conditions arise and you cannot communicate or decide Typically when you cannot make healthcare decisions yourself, depending on state law and document terms Depends on drafting; may take effect immediately or upon incapacity


The documents can therefore complement one another. An advance directive gives specific guidance. Meanwhile, a healthcare agent is there to address situations that were impossible to anticipate ahead of time.


## Why You May Need Both Documents


An advance directive alone may not cover every medical situation you could face. Even a detailed document cannot predict every diagnosis, treatment option or decision that may arise years later. A healthcare power of attorney fills that gap by giving a trusted person the authority to make decisions when your written instructions do not provide a clear answer.


A financial power of attorney serves an entirely different purpose. If you become incapacitated, someone may still need to pay your mortgage, manage investments, handle insurance claims, access bank accounts or deal with tax matters. An advance directive and healthcare POA generally do not give someone authority to perform those financial tasks.


For that reason, a comprehensive estate plan may include an advance directive, a healthcare power of attorney and a durable financial power of attorney. Together, they can address both your medical preferences and the practical financial decisions that may arise during a period of incapacity.


State law plays an important role in the structuring of these documents. Some states combine living-will instructions and healthcare-agent appointments into a single advance directive form. Others treat them as separate documents. Signing, witnessing and notarization requirements can also vary depending on the specific state.


An e[state planning attorney](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/estate-planning-attorney) can help determine which documents apply where you live. Further, they can ensure they work together instead of creating gaps or conflicting instructions. Putting these documents in place before they become necessary can give both your family and your chosen decision-makers clearer guidance if you eventually become unable to speak or act for yourself.


## Bottom Line


An advance directive and power of attorney serve different but complementary roles in an estate plan. An advance directive records your medical wishes. Meanwhile healthcare and financial powers of attorney appoint trusted people to make decisions when you cannot. Because state requirements vary, an estate planning attorney can help ensure these documents are properly drafted and work together without leaving important gaps.
